newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan offers high returns for forex depositors.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan offers high returns for forex depositors.

text.p: Pakistan's central bank on Tuesday announced attractive interest rates to bolster the patriotism of foreign currency depositors responding to Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's plan to tackle the national debt.
Some bankers said the rates were unnecessarily high and would add to Pakistan's overall debt problems.
"The problem is that it is very expensive borrowing," said Haroon Sharif, managing director of InterAsia Leasing Co Ltd.
"If the prime minister wanted to raise money from abroad at this time, people would have given for Pakistan. They do not need to attract expatriates with higher rates," he said.

Sharif, sworn in as prime minister on February 16 after winning February 3 elections, appealed on Sunday to an estimated two million expatriate Pakistanis to help sink the $30 billion foreign debt by sending their savings home through banks.
A State (central) Bank of Pakistan (SBP) statement said Pakistanis abroad were being asked to remit deposits of at least $1,000 each and additional amounts in multiples of $500.
Interest-bearing deposits, for a minimum of two years, would be mobilised in dollars, sterling and deutsche marks.
The SBP said resident Pakistanis could help by converting their short-term forex deposits, buying foreign currency notes or travellers cheques, or arranging remittances from abroad.
It said such deposits and interest were exempt from tax, bank commissions and deduction of Zakat, an Islamic tax.
The SBP announced the following annualised interest rates on foreign currency deposits, payable quarterly:
Currency Two-year Three-year Four-year Five-year
Dollar 7.50 pct 8.00 pct 8.50 pct 9.00 pct
Sterling 8.40 pct 8.80 pct 9.20 pct 9.75 pct
D-mark 5.10 pct 5.70 pct 6.30 pct 7.00 pct

Sharif, an industrialist, has taken over formidable economic problems from the caretaker administration installed after President Farooq Leghari sacked Benazir Bhutto's government last November 5 for alleged corruption and abuse of power.
Pakistan faces foreign debt repayments totalling about $1.5 billion in March to June, not including payments on military debt. Liquid foreign reserves now stand at $792 million.
In his first address to the nation on Sunday, Sharif said his government had to find unconventional methods to tackle the "smouldering heaps of destruction" it had inherited.
He said he could follow his predecessors and borrow heavily to meet foreign debt payments, but added: "I consider it a crime to obtain such loans which suck the blood of the masses."

Some analysts say Pakistan could gain a respite from its financial crisis if Sharif's appeal strikes a responsive chord, while others say the breathing-space could be all too short unless Pakistan can correct its chronic fiscal deficit.
"It is highly likely that the prime minister will be able to attract a net inflow of $1 billion from this scheme," said Kalim Aziz, head of research at ING Baring Securities.
"This will lend some breathing time to the government and help Pakistan solve its debt repayment problem. Success of this policy will also win some favour from the IMF," he said.
Ayesha Muzaffar, financial analyst at James Capel Asia, said the new scheme offered Pakistanis dollar interest rates two to three percent higher than those offered in the United States.
The deposits were also guaranteed by the SBP and were not subject to bank commissions, Muzaffar noted.
"I think the incentive is definitely there for a rational Pakistani investor to put money into these schemes," she said.

Non-resident Pakistanis could even arbitrage by borrowing from local banks at four percent and depositing the funds in these accounts. "But this is something new so it may take some time for Pakistani investors to get onto this," she said.
